slides.0.title: Sparkling wines of England and the New World
slides.0.subtitle: Warming moves the sparkling map north, south and uphill
slides.1.title: England
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Terroir
slides.1.highlights.0.content: The south-east (Sussex, Kent, Hampshire) has chalk from the same geological band as Champagne, along with greensand and other soils; a cool, marginal maritime climate gives high-acid base wines ideal for sparkling
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Risks
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Spring frost, cold rain at flowering and incomplete ripening make yields swing from year to year; warming has made ripening more reliable, part of the background to English sparkling wine’s rise over the last two decades
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Sussex PDO and Champagne investment
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Sussex gained PDO status in 2022, the UK’s first sub-regional PDO; Champagne houses have invested too, such as Taittinger’s Domaine Evremond in Kent, a sign of confidence in English terroir
slides.1.content: England’s story: marginal climate + chalk + warming + capital = a new top sparkling region.
slides.2.title: The traditional method in the New World
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Tasmania
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Australia’s coolest region, regarded as the heart of its top traditional-method sparkling wine; mainland houses have long sourced base wine here
slides.2.highlights.1.title: California
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Champagne houses set up in California from the 1970s–80s, such as Moët’s Domaine Chandon (Napa) and Roederer Estate (Anderson Valley); cool Carneros and Anderson Valley are key sources of base wine
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Other regions
slides.2.highlights.2.content: New Zealand’s Marlborough also makes traditional-method sparkling; South Africa’s Cap Classique needs at least 12 months on the lees (from the 2023 vintage) and whole-bunch pressing; Argentina’s altitude and Chandon (founded 1959) are important cases too
slides.2.content: Champagne houses investing abroad is itself a good D4 example: exporting brand, know-how and a terroir search.
slides.3.title: Essay angle: how new regions compete
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Cost and price
slides.3.highlights.0.content: New regions face high vineyard and equipment investment, volatile yields and capital tied up in long lees ageing, so prices often approach Champagne NV and must be justified by quality and story
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Names and recognition
slides.3.highlights.1.content: England and Tasmania are building regional names (such as the Sussex PDO); the clearer the name, the easier it is to escape the “Champagne substitute” positioning
slides.3.highlights.2.title: The two sides of climate change
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Warming benefits marginal regions such as England but makes it harder for warm regions to keep acidity; cover both sides in essays
slides.3.content: Skeleton for new-region questions: conditions (climate, soil) → investment (capital, know-how) → market (name, price) → risks.
